props.title: Alice Doesn't Live Here Anymore
props.initialSlug: Waitress chases singing dreams while raising her son

sections.content: Martin Scorsese's Alice Doesn't Live Here Anymore marks a pivotal moment in 1970s American cinema, showcasing Ellen Burstyn's Oscar-winning performance as a widow pursuing her singing dreams while raising her son. The film blazed a trail for complex female narratives, arriving alongside other feminist landmarks like An Unmarried Woman (1978) and Woman Under the Influence (1974). Scorsese's raw direction captures both gritty realism and tender moments, proving his versatility beyond the male-dominated stories he'd become known for with Mean Streets (1973) and Taxi Driver (1976).

sections.content: The film's influence extended far beyond cinema, spawning the successful TV series "Alice" (1976-1985). Burstyn's Alice Hyatt became a template for depicting working-class single mothers with complexity and dignity, paving the way for films like Norma Rae (1979) and Places in the Heart (1984). The authentic portrayal of roadside diners and southwestern America's landscape creates a vivid backdrop that influenced later road movies like Paris, Texas (1984).

Kris Kristofferson's portrayal of David marks a shift in how male romantic leads were depicted in the 1970s - sensitive, flawed, and capable of growth. This characterization influenced later films like Urban Cowboy (1980) and Tender Mercies (1983), where masculine stereotypes gave way to more nuanced portrayals. movies.title: Norma Rae
movies.slug: A factory worker becomes involved in unionizing her textile mill

sections.content: The film belongs to a crucial wave of 1970s cinema that centered working-class women's experiences. Alongside Network (1976) and Nine to Five (1980), it portrayed workplace dynamics with unprecedented realism. The diner scenes, featuring Harvey Keitel and Diane Ladd, capture the camaraderie and tensions of service industry work with documentary-like authenticity.
